response.content: {"answer": "The four connection protocols are: OPENAI_COMPATIBLE (speaks the Chat Completions API), OPENAI_RESPONSES (speaks the Responses API), ANTHROPIC (speaks the Messages API), and GEMINI (speaks the Google Generative Language API).", "cited_ids": ["guide/connect-provider#1"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Keep the provider API key in the gitignored `.env` file at the repository root. In configuration, reference it with an `env:NAME` pointer (for example, the connection's credential reference names the environment variable holding the key) rather than pasting the secret into code, logs, traces, or recordings. Shared presets live in `config/providers.toml`, and that file holds only the `env:NAME` pointer, which the secrets scanner treats as safe, so the config can be committed cleanly. The `resolve_credential` function reads the named variable at call time and returns the key value (or `None` for keyless connections), and only the credentials module and the live benchmark runner may touch the environment for a secret; other modules receive the value as an argument.", "cited_ids": ["guide/connect-provider#0", "guide/connect-provider#2", "guide/connect-provider#1"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "For every connection, `wam doctor` prints one row with the connection's id, protocol, outcome, and latency in milliseconds. The outcome can be one of: `OK`, `CONFIG_INVALID`, `CREDENTIAL_MISSING`, `CREDENTIAL_REJECTED`, `ENDPOINT_UNREACHABLE`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `PROTOCOL_UNSUPPORTED`, or `UNKNOWN`.", "cited_ids": ["guide/connect-provider#3"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "`resolve_credential` resolves the credential reference into a real key. It reads the named variable at call time and returns the key value, or `None` for keyless connections. Only the credentials module and the live benchmark runner may read a secret from the environment. Every other module receives the value as an argument and must never print, log, or store it in a trace.", "cited_ids": ["guide/connect-provider#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Build the chat model with `make_chat_model(connection, model_id)` from `which_ai_model.core`, passing a connection obtained via `get_connection(id, load_connections())`. Never construct the provider class by hand. The class is chosen by protocol: `OPENAI_COMPATIBLE` gets `ChatOpenAI`; `OPENAI_RESPONSES` gets `ChatOpenAI` in Responses mode; `ANTHROPIC` gets `ChatAnthropic`; and `GEMINI` gets `ChatGoogleGenerativeAI`.", "cited_ids": ["guide/call-model-schema#1", "guide/call-model-schema#0", "guide/connect-provider#1"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Wrap the chat model with your pydantic schema using make_structured_model(model, YourSchema) (which uses the function_calling strategy), then call it with include_raw=True. On success you get the parsed pydantic object. If validation fails, you don't get an exception: with include_raw=True the failure arrives as data, a parsing_error value next to a None parse, and the runner records schema_valid=False while keeping the raw content for diagnosis.", "cited_ids": ["guide/call-model-schema#2", "guide/call-model-schema#0", "guide/tracing#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "The shared data shapes are pydantic models defined in `contracts.py`: `RouteOut` (one intent label) for routing, `ScopeOut` (an out-of-scope flag) for scope, `ReplyOut` (an intent, an urgency level, and the reply text) for replies, and `DocsOut` (an answer, the cited passage ids, and an abstention flag) for docs. They are better than regex extraction because the schema is a real type, so a malformed answer is a validation error that can be counted, rather than a formatting surprise discovered on the page. Every tool asks the model for structured data instead of free text parsed with a prompt or regular expression, and one shared helper wraps any provider class with these schemas, so tool code never branches on providers and benchmark calls stay comparable.", "cited_ids": ["guide/call-model-schema#0", "guide/langgraph-flow#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "A tool is a plain Python function with a typed signature and a docstring, wrapped so the model can call it during a run. Keep argument types simple (strings, numbers, booleans, and small pydantic models), and return either a scalar or a small dictionary the agent can quote back. Fallback and retry logic does not go inside the tool; it is attached once at agent construction as middleware. The docstring matters more than usual because it becomes the tool description the model reads when deciding what to call. It should be written as an instruction that says when to use the tool and what each argument means.", "cited_ids": ["guide/add-tool#0"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Assemble the tools into an agent with `create_agent` from the installed `langchain` package, passing `model`, `tools=[...]`, and a `system_prompt`. It returns a compiled graph that you invoke with a message list, e.g. `result = await agent.ainvoke({\"messages\": [{\"role\": \"user\", \"content\": question}]})`. Use the asynchronous `ainvoke` form rather than synchronous calls: some tool sources are async-only and raise on synchronous calls, so awaiting everywhere keeps every tool working through the same path. (MCP tools specifically raise `NotImplementedError` on `invoke`, so use `ainvoke` for them as well.) Retry and fallback behavior is attached at agent construction as middleware, not inside the tools.", "cited_ids": ["guide/add-tool#1", "guide/add-tool#0", "guide/mcp-tools#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Expose new functions by decorating plain Python functions with `@server.tool()` on an `MCPServer` instance (imported from `mcp.server.mcpserver`, named e.g. \"fee-tools\"), then expose them through the project's builder `build_mcp_server()` in `tools/mcp_server.py`. Build them on the `MCPServer` class. Clients then load them with `MCPAdapter` (from `langchain.mcp`), remembering that MCP tools are async-only (use `ainvoke`) and return content blocks that must be parsed.", "cited_ids": ["guide/mcp-tools#1", "guide/mcp-tools#2", "guide/new-tool-template#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Configure fallback and retry at agent construction, as middleware, not inside the tool function. The fallback switches to a second model instance on transport failures; pass model instances built from Connection objects so the fallback keeps its base URL, key reference, and headers. The retry policy has a small retry count with exponential backoff and an error outcome that raises. Fallback and retry trigger only on transport problems such as rate limits and unreachable endpoints. A slow or wrong tool result is returned to the model as an observation, and a schema-invalid final answer is scored, not re-requested.", "cited_ids": ["guide/add-tool#2", "guide/add-tool#0"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Use `MCPAdapter` from `langchain.mcp` as an async context manager, passing a `Path` object to the server script (a plain string must be an http(s) URL). Inside the block, call `tools = await adapter.list_tools()` to enumerate the tools. The adapter closes the subprocess when the block exits. Note that MCP tools are async-only, so call them with `ainvoke`, and tool calls return a list of MCP content blocks that you need to parse for the text value.", "cited_ids": ["guide/mcp-tools#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Calling `invoke` on an MCP tool raises `NotImplementedError`, because MCP tools are async-only; use `ainvoke` instead, and drive the agent with `ainvoke` too. A successful tool call returns a list of MCP content blocks, which are dictionaries with `type`, `text`, and an id, not a plain Python value. You parse the text block to recover the scalar.", "cited_ids": ["guide/mcp-tools#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "In the docs flow, retrieval, generation, and citation run as three steps in order: retrieve, then answer, then cite. Retrieval queries the passage store built by `make rag-index`. Answering calls the model with those passages in context, through `answer_question`, which returns a `DocsOut` object. Citing attaches the passage ids the answer actually used. Citations are plain strings of the form `guide/<page>#<n>` carried through the state. Verification happens in the final node, which checks that every cited id was really retrieved. If the guide cannot answer a question, the flow sets `abstained=True` with an empty citation list instead of guessing.", "cited_ids": ["guide/langgraph-flow#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Declare the state shape as a TypedDict, add one node per step (each node maps state to a dict of updates), wire the edges with plain edges from START and conditional edges for branching, then compile the StateGraph and invoke it with the initial state. Keep node functions pure, route model calls through the shared model layer, and add a checkpointer only if the flow must pause and resume.", "cited_ids": ["guide/langgraph-flow#0", "guide/langgraph-flow#1"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "The flow should return an explicit refusal: it sets `abstained=True` with an empty citation list instead of guessing or fabricating an answer.", "cited_ids": ["guide/langgraph-flow#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Each row (one CallRecord) records: run id, task name, tool name, item id, model reference (connection id plus model id), prompt version, wall-clock latency in milliseconds, input and output token counts, dollar cost, whether the output validated against its schema, the error class on failure, and the recording key that locates the raw response. Failed calls are also written, with the error field set and the schema flag empty.", "cited_ids": ["guide/tracing#1", "guide/tracing#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "The callback handler, passed via config={\"callbacks\": [...]}, runs on model end. It reads the first generation's message, takes token counts from its usage_metadata, takes the finish reason from response metadata, and takes the model name from the result output, then appends one scrubbed JSON row. Key material, headers, and credential-bearing URLs are never allowed into the row, which carries only counts, the finish reason, and identifiers. Rows are the JSON form of the CallRecord pydantic contract, and readers validate each line against it, rejecting corrupt files loudly. For totals only, the standard UsageMetadataCallbackHandler can aggregate input, output, and total tokens.", "cited_ids": ["guide/tracing#2", "guide/tracing#1"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "A structured call is schema-valid exactly when the `parsing_error` returned with `include_raw=True` is `None`; the trace row's schema flag reflects this (`schema_valid=False` on a parse failure). Yes, failed calls are kept in the trace file: every model call appends exactly one row whether it succeeded or failed, with the error field set and the schema flag empty.", "cited_ids": ["guide/tracing#2", "guide/call-model-schema#2", "guide/tracing#0"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Record live traffic only during the one explicit live benchmark run and during deliberately live debugging; replay everywhere else, including all tests, where recorded fixtures stand in for the network. Replay is the default for everything run through make (WAM_MODE=replay), so make all rebuilds results byte-identically without a key or network. A cache miss (replay miss) is a signal that the prompt, model, or input changed without a matching recording; it means you should re-record deliberately, and you must never fall back to a live call inside a replay-mode run.", "cited_ids": ["guide/record-replay#0", "guide/record-replay#2", "guide/benchmark#3"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "The request digest is the sha256 of the canonical JSON of the request messages (sorted keys, no whitespace). The recording key is then the sha256 of the model id, the prompt version, and that digest joined with newlines.", "cited_ids": ["guide/record-replay#1"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "One row in the recordings directory is one JSONL row per model call. It holds the recording key, the model id, the prompt version, the request digest, a response object (content, tool calls, and scrubbed provider usage), and the UTC timestamp. The passages say the usage portion never carries headers, keys, or credential URLs.", "cited_ids": ["guide/record-replay#1"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "The benchmark has four tasks, all scored on the same frozen prompts:

1. **Routing messages to intents:** 616 items. These are 8 messages per intent drawn from the Banking77 test split.
2. **Out-of-scope detection:** 300 items, made up of 150 out-of-scope and 150 in-scope messages.
3. **Drafting structured replies:** 150 items, a seeded subset of the routing sample.
4. **Answering docs questions with citations:** the passages give no total item count and do not say where these samples come from. They mention only five unanswerable questions within this task.

All samples are stratified and seeded with `20261028`, and the committed id lists live under `data/samples/`.", "cited_ids": ["guide/benchmark#0", "guide/benchmark#1", "guide/benchmark#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "The runner caps itself at 2 concurrent requests and 30 requests per minute per model. It also uses backoff that honours Retry-After, sends an identifying User-Agent and stable session header on each request, and halts immediately on any forbidden or abuse-style reply. When spending must stretch across rate-limit windows, it spreads the work over time rather than forcing it through.", "cited_ids": ["guide/cost-budget#2", "guide/benchmark#3"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "They are scored as wrong, with the reason recorded. An empty, cut-off, or unparseable answer is scored wrong and is never retried, and it does not crash the run. For structured replies, a parse failure is recorded as schema_valid=False while the raw content is kept for diagnosis, and the framework does not silently repair it.", "cited_ids": ["guide/benchmark#0", "guide/call-model-schema#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Routing reports accuracy and macro-F1 with a bootstrap 95% interval from 2,000 fixed-seed resamples; scope detection reports precision, recall, and F1 with Wilson intervals; replies report the schema-valid rate and the intent-correct rate among valid outputs; docs retrieval reports hit@4, citation precision, and correct abstention on five unanswerable questions. Scoring is fully rule-based because every score is deterministic and no model judges another model.", "cited_ids": ["guide/benchmark#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "The regression gate rejects a replacement model when either (1) its primary metric (macro-F1 for routing, F1 for scope detection, intent-correct rate for replies, hit@4 for docs) drops by more than 2.0 points on any task compared with the baseline, or (2) its reply schema-valid rate drops below 98%. Separately, it refuses to compare (which fails the command, though it is not a pass) when the sample hash, prompt version, or scorer version differ between baseline and candidate runs.", "cited_ids": ["guide/gate#1", "guide/gate#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "The gate refuses to compare two runs when their sample hash, prompt version, or scorer version differ between baseline and candidate, because the comparison would be meaningless. A refusal is not a pass: it fails the command explicitly so no pipeline mistakes it for approval.", "cited_ids": ["guide/gate#2", "guide/benchmark#1"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Import `check_gate` from `which_ai_model.gate` and pass the baseline and candidate result directories as `Path` objects. It returns `(passed, reasons)`, where `passed` is a boolean and `reasons` is a list of human-readable strings, one per violated condition. Keep the accepted baseline in its own immutable directory, and write each candidate run to a fresh dated directory. Both runs must be replay runs scored by the same code.

```python
from pathlib import Path
from which_ai_model.gate import check_gate

passed, reasons = check_gate(Path("results/runs/baseline"), Path("results/runs/candidate"))
```

Run the gate before any model change, and when it passes, the candidate becomes the new baseline.", "cited_ids": ["guide/gate#2", "guide/gate#0"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "A model is \"good enough\" on a task when it is within 3.0 points of the best model on that task. The picker considers only those good-enough models and recommends the cheapest, the most accurate, and the fastest among them, breaking ties toward lower cost. The picker's inputs come from deterministic metrics: quality scores, latency percentiles, token counts (input, output, and reasoning), and cost per 1,000 items, which together let it trade quality, speed, and price.", "cited_ids": ["guide/gate#1", "guide/benchmark#2", "guide/cost-budget#0"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "The four pieces are: a module with a typed entry function, a pydantic output schema, a system prompt, and a parity test. Start by copying the closest existing tool (router, drafter, scope checker, or agent) rather than a blank file.", "cited_ids": ["guide/new-tool-template#0", "guide/new-tool-template#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "The documentation helper is the deliberate exception to the usual parity check. Its retrieval changes its answers by design, so an exact match against the legacy fixtures would be the wrong test. Instead, its check only requires answering all 10 fixture questions while citing at least one passage for each.", "cited_ids": ["guide/new-tool-template#2"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "A call's dollar cost is measured or looked up, never guessed. The runner first uses the gateway's per-response measured value if the response carries it. Otherwise it multiplies the counted tokens by the per-model rates in the prices table (config/prices.toml), and the helper cost_usd returns a float when a source exists. When neither source exists, the runner records None, which is displayed as unknown; callers treat None as unknown all the way to the page, with no fallback constant or fudge factor.", "cited_ids": ["guide/cost-budget#0", "guide/cost-budget#1", "guide/tracing#1"], "abstained": false}

{"answer": "Write a parity test first and run it in replay mode against a fixed 50-item fixture set that is committed to the repo. Use a fake model that returns the legacy fixture's raw content. The new tool must match the legacy twin on the same label for classification, the same parsed fields for the drafter, and the same tool-call sequence and final answer for the agent. The docs helper is the exception: it must answer all 10 fixture questions and cite at least one passage for each. When the test passes with zero network calls, the tool is ready for the live run and the gate.", "cited_ids": ["guide/new-tool-template#2", "guide/record-replay#2"], "abstained": false}
{"answer": "The passages do not mention any editor plugins for syntax highlighting of prompt templates, so this question cannot be answered from them.", "cited_ids": [], "abstained": true}
{"answer": "", "cited_ids": [], "abstained": true}

{"answer": "The mechanism is a pre-cell cost estimate checked against the remaining budget in config/budget.toml: before each model-by-task cell, the runner estimates cost from sample size and locked prices, and the whole run has a hard spending cap that it never exceeds. When money runs short, the first step is to shrink the most expensive routing sample first (from 8 to 5 messages per intent), then the next most expensive model, recording the reduction as a deviation. If even the reduced plan would overspend, the run stops instead of spending.", "cited_ids": ["guide/cost-budget#2"], "abstained": false}
